questions.prompt: Write \(3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+5\mathbf k\) as coordinates in the standard basis.
questions.answer: The coefficients of \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) are the coordinates, so the vector is \((3,-2,5)\).

questions.prompt: Express \((4,-1)\) as a combination of \(\mathbf i\) and \(\mathbf j\).
questions.answer: Use the standard basis: \((4,-1)=4\mathbf i-\mathbf j\).

questions.prompt: For basis \(\mathbf b_1=(1,1)\), \(\mathbf b_2=(1,-1)\), find coordinates of \(\mathbf v=(6,2)\).
Reconstruct a vector with basis coordinates \([3,-1]_B\) for \(B=((2,0),(1,1))\).
Find the magnitude of \(2\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+6\mathbf k\).
questions.answer: The coordinate vector is \((2,-3,6)\). Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{4+9+36}=7\).

questions.prompt: Find the standard coordinates of \(2\mathbf b_1+5\mathbf b_2\) where \(\mathbf b_1=(1,0,1)\), \(\mathbf b_2=(0,1,-1)\).
For \(B=((1,2),(3,1))\), find \([\mathbf v]_B\) when \(\mathbf v=(7,8)\).
Show that \((1,2)\) and \((2,4)\) do not form a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).
questions.answer: The second vector is \(2\) times the first, so the two vectors are parallel. They cannot span all directions in \(\mathbb R^2\).

questions.prompt: Find coordinates of \(\mathbf v=(3,4,5)\) in basis \(\mathbf e_1=(1,0,0)\), \(\mathbf e_2=(0,1,0)\), \(\mathbf e_3=(0,0,1)\).
questions.answer: This is the standard basis, so the coordinates are exactly \([3,4,5]\).
Equations are \(2a-b=3\) and \(a+b=5\). Adding gives \(3a=8\), so \(a=8/3\), and \(b=7/3\).

questions.prompt: Decompose \((5,5)\) into components parallel to \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\).
Convert polar components \(6\) at angle \(60^\circ\) into standard basis components.
questions.answer: The components are \((6\cos60^\circ,6\sin60^\circ)=(3,3\sqrt3)\).

questions.prompt: For \(B=((1,0),(1,1))\), convert standard vector \((2,5)\) to \(B\)-coordinates.
questions.answer: Solve \(a(1,0)+b(1,1)=(2,5)\). From the second component \(b=5\), then \(a+5=2\), so \(a=-3\).

questions.prompt: For \(B=((2,0),(0,3))\), find the standard vector with coordinates \([4,-2]_B\).
Check whether \((1,0,1),(0,1,1),(1,1,2)\) is a basis of \(\mathbb R^3\).
questions.answer: The third vector equals the sum of the first two, so the set is linearly dependent and is not a basis.

questions.prompt: Find the coordinate vector of \(\mathbf v=(0,7)\) in basis \(B=((1,1),(-1,1))\).
Find the orthonormal-basis coordinates of \(\mathbf v=(2,3)\) in basis \(\mathbf u_1=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)\), \(\mathbf u_2=(1/\sqrt2,-1/\sqrt2)\).
questions.answer: Coordinates are dot products: \(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u_1=5/\sqrt2\) and \(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u_2=-1/\sqrt2\).

questions.prompt: A vector has coordinates \([1,2,3]_B\) with \(B=((1,0,0),(1,1,0),(1,1,1))\). Find standard coordinates, then recover the \(B\)-coordinates from your result.
questions.answer: Convert to standard coordinates: \(1(1,0,0)+2(1,1,0)+3(1,1,1)=(6,5,3)\). To recover coordinates, solve \(a(1,0,0)+b(1,1,0)+c(1,1,1)=(6,5,3)\). The third component gives \(c=3\), the second gives \(b+c=5\), so \(b=2\), and the first gives \(a+b+c=6\), so \(a=1\).

questions.prompt: A student claims \([2,c]_{((1,2),(3,4))}\) represents \((11,16)\). Find \(c\) from the \(x\)-component and use the \(y\)-component to check whether the claim is consistent.
questions.answer: The represented vector is \(2(1,2)+c(3,4)=(2+3c,4+4c)\). From the \(x\)-component, \(2+3c=11\), so \(c=3\). The \(y\)-component would then be \(4+4(3)=16\), matching the claimed vector. The claim is consistent and \(c=3\).

questions.prompt: Find the change-of-basis coordinates of \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) in basis \(((1,1),(1,-1))\), then use them to express \((3,-2)\) in that basis.
